subject: Civil Engineering
title: Bridge Loads: What a Bridge Must Carry
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Bridge Loads: What a Bridge Must Carry.

hook.text: A highway bridge must carry its own weight, traffic, wind, and sometimes ice.

buildup.text: Dead load is the bridge itself. Live load is everything moving across it.

discovery.text: Dynamic loads from trucks bounce — impact factors multiply the static weight.

twist.text: Thermal expansion can add huge forces. Bridges grow inches longer in summer heat.

climax.text: Expansion joints and roller bearings let the bridge move without cracking.

punchline.text: A bridge must carry everything — including the weather.

quiz.question: Why do bridges have expansion joints?
options: To make the bridge easier to disassemble for repairs
To allow the bridge to expand and contract with temperature changes
To reduce the total weight of the bridge deck

details.summary: Bridge loads include dead loads from the structure's own weight, live loads from traffic and pedestrians, environmental loads from wind, earthquakes, and temperature changes, and accidental loads from vehicle collisions or vessel strikes. Engineers must design for all combinations simultaneously.
details.whyItMatters: Underestimating any load type can lead to bridge failure. Modern codes require engineers to consider dozens of load combinations to ensure safety under all foreseeable conditions.
takeaways: Dead loads are the permanent weight of the bridge structure itself
Live loads include vehicles, pedestrians, and temporary construction loads
Environmental loads from wind, seismic, and thermal effects must all be considered

faq.question: Which type of load is usually most critical for bridge design?
faq.answer: It depends on the bridge type. For short-span highway bridges, truck live loads often govern design. For long-span suspension bridges, wind loads dominate. In seismic zones, earthquake forces may control the design of piers and foundations.

faq.question: How do engineers account for loads they cannot precisely predict?
faq.answer: Engineers apply load factors that multiply estimated loads by safety margins, typically 1.2 to 1.75 depending on load type. They also use load combinations that consider the probability of multiple extreme loads occurring simultaneously, following codes like AASHTO LRFD.
